We reserve all rights and objections.

**MR. HARWICK:** Understood, Ms. Pendleton. Thank you. Let\'s begin.

**[1.3 Background Identification of Witness]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, let me start with some basic background information. Can you please state your full name for the record?

**DR. HALPERN:** Marcus Alan Halpern.

**MR. HARWICK:** And what is your current home address?

**DR. HALPERN:** 1842 Lakeview Terrace, Winnetka, Illinois 60093.

**MR. HARWICK:** What was your most recent position at Crestline Therapeutics?

**DR. HALPERN:** I was the Chief Financial Officer.

**MR. HARWICK:** When did you begin in that role?

**DR. HALPERN:** I joined Crestline in the spring of 2018. Officially, my start date was in March 2018, I believe, but it was --- it was that spring timeframe.

**MR. HARWICK:** And when did you leave?

**DR. HALPERN:** I resigned on September 14, 2023. That was my last day.

**MR. HARWICK:** So you were CFO from approximately March 2018 through September 14, 2023?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct.

**MR. HARWICK:** Can you briefly describe your educational background and professional credentials?

**DR. HALPERN:** Sure. I have an MBA from the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University. I am also a licensed Certified Public Accountant in the State of Illinois. My license number is 065-041882.

**MR. HARWICK:** And before joining Crestline, where were you employed?

**DR. HALPERN:** Before Crestline, I was Vice President of Finance at Praxon Medical Devices. I was there from 2011 to 2018. Before that, I held various roles in finance and accounting at a couple of different companies, but Praxon was where I was immediately before coming to Crestline.

**MR. HARWICK:** What was your compensation at Crestline?

**DR. HALPERN:** My base salary was \$485,000 per year. My target annual bonus was 60 percent of base, which works out to approximately \$291,000. I also received equity awards --- stock options and restricted stock units --- as part of my compensation package.

**MR. HARWICK:** Are you currently employed?

**DR. HALPERN:** No, I am currently unemployed.

**MR. HARWICK:** Can you describe your responsibilities as CFO of Crestline?

**DR. HALPERN:** As CFO, I had overall responsibility for the company\'s finance, accounting, financial reporting, treasury, tax, and investor relations functions. Essentially, everything that fell under the finance umbrella reported to me. I reported directly to the Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Anya Petrova, and I also had a dotted-line reporting relationship to the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors.

**MR. HARWICK:** Who were your direct reports?

**DR. HALPERN:** My primary direct reports included Janet Liang, who was the Vice President of Revenue Operations and also served as the Corporate Controller. There was Derek Yoon, who was the Director of Financial Reporting. I also had direct reports in treasury and tax, but Janet and Derek were the two most relevant to the financial reporting and revenue recognition areas that I expect are the focus of today\'s discussion.

**MR. HARWICK:** Thank you. Let\'s turn to the substance of the investigation.

**[II. OVERVIEW OF REVENUE RECOGNITION PROCESS AT CRESTLINE]{.underline}**

**[2.1 General Revenue Recognition Framework]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to start by asking you to describe, in general terms, Crestline\'s approach to revenue recognition for its partnership and collaboration agreements. Can you walk me through the process?

**DR. HALPERN:** Of course. Crestline applied ASC 606, which is the accounting standard for Revenue from Contracts with Customers, to all of its significant revenue arrangements. That was the governing standard, and we were very focused on making sure we applied it correctly.

The way the process worked was that for every significant arrangement --- and by that I mean our partnership agreements, our collaboration agreements, our licensing agreements --- the finance team would prepare what we called a revenue recognition memorandum. These memos would walk through the five-step model that ASC 606 prescribes. Step one is identifying the contract with the customer. Step two is identifying the distinct performance obligations within that contract. Step three is determining the transaction price. Step four is allocating the transaction price to the individual performance obligations. And step five is recognizing revenue when, or as, each performance obligation is satisfied. That five-step framework was the backbone of our analysis for every significant transaction.

The initial drafting of these memos was typically done by Derek Yoon and his team in financial reporting, working closely with Janet Liang\'s revenue operations group. Janet\'s team was responsible for understanding the operational details of the agreements --- what was being delivered, when milestones were achieved, what the contractual triggers were. Derek\'s group would then translate that operational understanding into the accounting analysis.

I had a very hands-on management style when it came to revenue recognition. As CFO, I personally reviewed every revenue recognition memo before it was finalized. These were among the most consequential accounting judgments we made, and I took that responsibility very seriously. I didn\'t sign off on anything without reading it carefully and making sure I understood the analysis and was comfortable with the conclusions.

Once the memos were finalized, they would be discussed with our outside auditors at Stanton Barrow & Co. during the quarterly review process and as part of the annual audit. The engagement partner at Stanton Barrow was Richard Muñoz, CPA. Richard was someone I worked closely with on accounting matters throughout my tenure at Crestline. We had a good professional relationship, and I valued his input on these complex judgments.

**MR. HARWICK:** When you say you \"worked closely\" with Mr. Muñoz, can you elaborate on what that means?

**DR. HALPERN:** What I mean is that Richard was our primary point of contact at the audit firm for all significant accounting matters. If there was a complex revenue recognition question, or any area that required significant judgment, I would typically discuss it with Richard directly. We had regular touchpoints --- quarterly at a minimum --- and then ad hoc consultations as issues arose. It was a professional working relationship. He understood our business, and I found his perspective useful.

**MR. HARWICK:** Thank you. Let\'s talk more specifically about Stanton Barrow\'s role.

**[2.2 Interaction with Outside Auditors --- Stanton Barrow & Co.]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, can you describe in more detail how the company interacted with Stanton Barrow on revenue recognition matters?

**DR. HALPERN:** Absolutely. I consulted extensively with Stanton Barrow on every significant revenue recognition judgment. Every material accounting treatment went through them, and they signed off on all treatments. I would not have been comfortable recognizing revenue on any significant transaction without their concurrence. That was the standard I held myself to as CFO.

The cadence of our interactions was as follows: We had quarterly review meetings where we would discuss the financial results for the period, including any significant revenue recognition items. In between quarters, if a new transaction came up or a complex judgment arose, we would consult with Stanton Barrow on an interim basis. There were also real-time discussions on judgmental areas --- for instance, if there was a question about whether a milestone had been achieved or how to allocate transaction price, we would pick up the phone or send an email and get their input before finalizing our position.

I personally presented the key revenue recognition positions to Richard Muñoz and his audit team. This was not something I delegated. When it came to the significant judgments --- the ones that could move the needle on our financial results --- I was the one sitting across the table from the auditors, walking them through our analysis, and making sure they understood the facts and the reasoning.

**MR. HARWICK:** And with respect to the two transactions that are a focus of this investigation --- the Meridian BioSciences Partnership Agreement and the Aethon Pharma Co-Development Agreement --- was Stanton Barrow aware of both of those?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes, absolutely. Stanton Barrow was aware of the Meridian Agreement and the Aethon Agreement. They reviewed both transactions thoroughly. Both were significant revenue arrangements, and both went through the full audit and review process that I\'ve described. Richard Muñoz and his team had access to the revenue recognition memos, the underlying contracts, and the supporting documentation for both transactions.

**MR. HARWICK:** And Stanton Barrow issued unqualified opinions on the company\'s financial statements for both FY2021 and FY2022?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct. Clean opinions for both years. We did everything by the book. Stanton Barrow reviewed it, they audited it, and they issued clean opinions. I had confidence in the integrity of the financial statements, and so did our auditors.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did Stanton Barrow ever express reservations or concerns about any of the revenue recognition treatments we\'ve discussed?

**DR. HALPERN:** Not to my recollection. We had healthy discussions, as you would expect --- the auditors pushed back on certain assumptions from time to time, asked clarifying questions, requested additional documentation. That\'s what good auditors do. But at the end of the day, they were comfortable with the treatments we applied, and they signed off.

**[2.3 Role of General Counsel in Revenue Recognition]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** I\'d like to ask about the role of the General Counsel in revenue recognition decisions. The General Counsel at Crestline was Rob Falcone, correct?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct. Rob Falcone was the General Counsel.

**MR. HARWICK:** What was Mr. Falcone\'s role, if any, in the revenue recognition process?

**DR. HALPERN:** Rob was involved in reviewing the legal aspects of our partnership and collaboration agreements. When it came to revenue recognition, there are often questions that require legal interpretation --- for example, what does a particular contract term mean? Has a contractual milestone been satisfied from a legal standpoint? Is a particular payment structure consistent with the company\'s legal obligations? Those are the types of questions where Rob\'s input was essential.

So the way it typically worked was that our finance team would prepare the revenue recognition analysis, and if there were legal questions embedded in that analysis --- and there almost always were --- we would involve Rob. He would review the relevant contract provisions, provide his interpretation, and that legal interpretation would then be incorporated into the revenue recognition memo.

**MR. HARWICK:** And was Mr. Falcone generally in agreement with the revenue recognition positions that the company took?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Rob was fully supportive of all the revenue recognition positions we took. He reviewed the agreements, he understood the economics, and he was comfortable with how we were accounting for these transactions. There was never any disagreement between Rob and me on these matters. We worked well together, and I valued his legal judgment.

**MR. HARWICK:** I want to ask specifically about his involvement in the Aethon territorial option analysis. Was Mr. Falcone involved in that?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes, he was. In fact, the territorial option question was one where Rob\'s involvement was particularly important, because the question of whether Aethon had constructively exercised its territorial options was fundamentally a legal interpretation question. Rob weighed in on that --- he analyzed the contract language, he reviewed the email communications with Aethon, and he agreed with the position that the options had been constructively exercised. He was on board with that conclusion.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did Mr. Falcone ever express reservations about any revenue recognition treatment at Crestline?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. Not that I recall. Rob was on board. As I said, we had a collaborative working relationship. He understood the accounting implications of his legal conclusions, and he was always thoughtful and diligent. But in terms of disagreements or reservations, no --- I don\'t recall any.

**MR. HARWICK:** Thank you. Let\'s turn to the specific transactions.

**[III. MERIDIAN BIOSCIENCES PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT]{.underline}**

**[3.1 Overview of the Meridian Agreement]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to turn now to the Meridian BioSciences Partnership Agreement. Can you walk me through that transaction from the beginning?

**DR. HALPERN:** Sure. The Meridian BioSciences Partnership Agreement was a collaboration and licensing agreement focused on compound CRT-4400, which was one of Crestline\'s immuno-oncology treatment candidates. The agreement was executed on June 15, 2021.

The total deal value was approximately \$38 million. The structure of the deal was as follows: There was a \$12 million upfront license fee, which we characterized as a technology access payment --- essentially, Meridian was paying for the right to access and use our intellectual property related to CRT-4400. Then there were \$8 million in milestone payments tied to Phase II clinical trial enrollment targets. And finally, there was \$18 million in co-development cost-sharing obligations that would be payable over the life of the collaboration as certain development activities were conducted.

Patricia Simmons, our Head of Business Development, led the negotiation of the agreement. She was the primary business-side contact with Meridian. I was involved in the financial structuring of the deal --- working with Patricia on the payment terms, the milestone definitions, and the overall economics. I also participated in some of the negotiation sessions, particularly the ones that dealt with financial terms.

**MR. HARWICK:** And the \$12 million upfront fee --- was that a one-time payment upon execution?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. The \$12 million was payable upon execution of the agreement, and it was received in full in late June 2021.

**[3.2 Recognition of \$12 Million Upfront Fee (Q2 2021)]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** How did the company account for that \$12 million upfront payment?

**DR. HALPERN:** We recognized the full \$12 million in revenue in Q2 2021, upon execution of the agreement. The ASC 606 analysis concluded that the license component of the Meridian agreement constituted a transfer of functional intellectual property. Under ASC 606, when a license grants the customer a right to use the entity\'s intellectual property as it exists at the point in time the license is granted --- what the standard calls functional intellectual property --- revenue is recognized at a point in time, which is when the license is transferred.

Our analysis concluded that Crestline had no further obligations related to the upfront fee after the license was transferred to Meridian. The technology access payment was distinct from the other performance obligations under the agreement --- the milestone-based development services and the cost-sharing arrangements were separate obligations with their own revenue recognition treatment.

This treatment was reviewed and approved by Stanton Barrow during the Q2 2021 quarterly review. I should note that this particular recognition --- the \$12 million upfront --- was later confirmed as appropriate and was not part of any restatement. It is my understanding that the Audit Committee\'s investigation has not identified any issues with the upfront fee recognition.

**MR. HARWICK:** That\'s correct. The \$12 million upfront recognition is not a subject of concern in this investigation. Let me turn to the milestone payment.

**[3.3 Recognition of \$5.2 Million Milestone (Q4 2021)]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to discuss the \$5.2 million milestone revenue that the company recognized in Q4 2021. This milestone was tied to Meridian\'s first-patient enrollment in the Phase II clinical trial for CRT-4400. Can you walk me through what happened?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Under the Meridian Agreement, there were several milestone payments tied to clini

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct. We recognized the \$5.2 million in Q4 2021.

**DR. HALPERN:** The milestone was confirmed to us in late November 2021 by the Meridian project manager. We received word that the first patient had been enrolled in the Phase II trial, and on that basis, we recognized the \$5.2 million as revenue in the fourth quarter of 2021.

**MR. HARWICK:** When you say \"confirmed to us,\" who specifically received this confirmation, and in what form?

**MR. HARWICK:** And what did your team do with that information?

**DR. HALPERN:** Derek Yoon prepared the revenue recognition memorandum for the \$5.2 million milestone. The memo analyzed the milestone under ASC 606, concluded that the performance obligation had been satisfied --- specifically, that first patient enrollment had occurred --- and recommended recognition of the \$5.2 million in Q4 2021. I reviewed and signed off on that memo on December 28, 2021.

**MR. HARWICK:** You reviewed and signed off on the memo on December 28, 2021?

**DR. HALPERN:** Correct.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did you personally verify the enrollment milestone with anyone at Meridian?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. I relied on the team. Patricia and her group were in regular contact with Meridian. The information we received indicated the milestone had been achieved. As CFO, I was making revenue recognition judgments based on the information that was brought to me by the people whose job it was to track these operational milestones. That\'s how the process worked.

**MR. HARWICK:** Were you aware at the time --- meaning in Q4 2021 --- that there were any questions about whether the enrollment milestone had been fully confirmed?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. At the time, I understood the milestone had been met. There was no ambiguity in the information I received. It wasn\'t until much later --- I believe during this investigation --- that I became aware there was any question about the timing.

**MR. HARWICK:** So you were not aware of any suggestion that the enrollment confirmation was preliminary or unconfirmed?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. I was not aware of that. The information that came to me indicated the milestone had been achieved. If there were caveats or qualifications attached to that information at the operational level, they were not communicated to me.

**MR. HARWICK:** And the revenue recognition memo prepared by Mr. Yoon --- did it reference any uncertainty about whether enrollment had actually occurred?

**DR. HALPERN:** Not that I recall. The memo concluded that the performance obligation was satisfied. If there had been any uncertainty flagged in the memo, I would have noticed it during my review, and I would have followed up on it. I reviewed these memos carefully.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did you have any conversations with anyone at Crestline about whether the enrollment milestone had actually been met by the end of Q4 2021?

**DR. HALPERN:** No, because there was nothing to discuss. The information was clear --- the milestone had been met.

**MR. HARWICK:** Thank you. Let me ask you about what happened subsequently.

**[3.4 Halpern\'s Understanding of the Restatement of the Meridian Milestone]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, the Audit Committee\'s investigation has identified concerns about the timing of this milestone recognition. Specifically, there is information suggesting that first patient enrollment in the Meridian Phase II trial may not have been confirmed until February 2022, rather than Q4 2021. Are you aware of that?

**DR. HALPERN:** I\'m aware of it now. As I said, I first became aware of questions about the timing when the Audit Committee investigation began. Prior to that, I had no reason to believe the milestone had not been achieved in Q4 2021.

**MR. HARWICK:** So your position is that at the time the \$5.2 million was recognized in Q4 2021, you believed in good faith that the enrollment milestone had been met?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s exactly right. The team acted in good faith based on the information available. If it turns out that the enrollment was not fully confirmed until February 2022, that\'s news to me as of this investigation. That was not my understanding at the time.

**MS. PENDLETON:** Mr. Harwick, I want to note for the record that my client is speaking based on his present recollection. He is cooperating fully, but he is not conceding any impropriety with respect to the revenue recognition treatment. If additional documents or information come to light that bear on this issue, we reserve the right to supplement his testimony.

**MR. HARWICK:** Noted. Thank you, Ms. Pendleton. Let\'s move on to the Aethon Pharma agreement.

**[IV. AETHON PHARMA CO-DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT]{.underline}**

**[4.1 Overview of the Aethon Agreement]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to turn now to the Aethon Pharma Co-Development Agreement. Can you describe that transaction?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. The Aethon Pharma Co-Development Agreement was executed on January 22, 2022. It was a co-development arrangement focused on certain immuno-oncology compounds in our pipeline. The deal was structured as a multi-component arrangement with a total deal value of approximately \$52 million.

**MR. HARWICK:** Can you break down the components for me?

**DR. HALPERN:** Sure. There were three principal components. First, a \$15 million upfront payment upon execution. Second, \$22 million in contingent milestone payments tied to various development and regulatory milestones. And third, \$15 million in option fees for ex-U.S. territorial rights --- meaning Aethon had the option to acquire rights to commercialize the compounds in certain territories outside the United States, and the aggregate value of those options was \$15 million.

**MR. HARWICK:** Who led the negotiations on the Crestline side?

**DR. HALPERN:** Again, Patricia Simmons led the business development negotiations. I was involved in the financial structuring, same as with Meridian. I worked closely with Patricia on the deal economics. Gregor Tannehill, our SVP of Commercial Operations, was also involved in the commercial aspects of the Aethon relationship --- he was focused on the market opportunity and the commercialization strategy for the compounds.

**MR. HARWICK:** And where was the agreement executed? Do you recall?

**DR. HALPERN:** It was signed at our offices. I don\'t recall the exact details of the signing --- whether it was a physical signing ceremony or done via electronic signature --- but it was finalized at our offices.

**MR. HARWICK:** Okay. Let\'s walk through the revenue recognition for the various components of the Aethon Agreement.

**[4.2 Recognition of \$15 Million Upfront Payment (Q1 2022)]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Starting with the \$15 million upfront payment. How was that accounted for?

**DR. HALPERN:** The \$15 million upfront was recognized in revenue in Q1 2022, upon execution of the agreement. The analysis was similar to what we did with the Meridian upfront. Under ASC 606, we identified the license component as a transfer of functional intellectual property. The license was distinct from the other performance obligations --- the co-development services and the territorial options. We concluded that Crestline had transferred the license at the point of execution and had no further obligations related to the upfront fee.

**MR. HARWICK:** And this was reviewed by Stanton Barrow?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Stanton Barrow reviewed the analysis during the Q1 2022 quarterly review and was comfortable with the treatment. This is another one that, to my understanding, has been determined to be appropriate and was not part of any restatement discussion.

**MR. HARWICK:** That\'s correct. The \$15 million upfront recognition is not a focus of this investigation. Let me turn to the compound delivery milestone.

**[4.3 Recognition of \$7.1 Million Compound Delivery Milestone (Q3 2022)]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to discuss the \$7.1 million milestone that the company recognized in Q3 2022, tied to compound delivery obligations. Can you walk me through that?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Under the Aethon Agreement, Crestline had an obligation to deliver certain compound batches to Aethon. These were physical compound materials that Aethon needed for its development work. The agreement specified that \$7.1 million in milestone payments would become recognizable upon delivery of compound materials to Aethon. Once the delivery obligations were met, Crestline had satisfied that performance obligation, and the revenue could be recognized.

**MR. HARWICK:** And the company recognized the \$7.1 million in Q3 2022?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct. We recognized the \$7.1 million in Q3 2022 because the compound delivery obligations had been met.

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, were you aware at any time during 2022 that compound delivery to Aethon was incomplete?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. I first learned that compound delivery to Aethon was incomplete when the Audit Committee investigation began in October 2023. That was the first time anyone brought to my attention that there was an issue with the completeness of the deliveries.

**MR. HARWICK:** So prior to October 2023, you had no information suggesting that all required compound batches had not been delivered to Aethon by the end of Q3 2022?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s correct. To my knowledge, the deliveries were complete. My team --- Janet Liang and her group --- would have been tracking the operational details. I had no reason to believe there was a problem.

**MR. HARWICK:** Let me make sure I understand your testimony. You are saying that between September 30, 2022, when Q3 closed, and October 2023, when the Audit Committee investigation began, no one at Crestline told you or communicated to you in any way that compound delivery to Aethon was incomplete or that there was any question about whether the delivery obligations had been fully satisfied?

**DR. HALPERN:** That\'s what I\'m saying. It never came to my attention. The revenue recognition memo prepared by Derek Yoon\'s group concluded that the delivery obligations were satisfied. I reviewed that memo and signed off on it. I had no reason to question the underlying facts.

**MR. HARWICK:** And just to be clear, you personally reviewed the Q3 2022 revenue recognition memo for the Aethon compound delivery milestone?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. As I mentioned, I personally reviewed every revenue recognition memo. The Q3 memo for the Aethon milestone concluded delivery was complete. That was the information I had, and I relied on it.

**[4.5 Recognition of \$8 Million Aethon Territorial Option Fee (Q4 2022)]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to discuss the \$8 million territorial option fee that the company recognized in Q4 2022. Can you explain that for me?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Under the Aethon Agreement, Aethon had options to acquire certain ex-U.S. territorial rights. The aggregate value of all the territorial options was \$15 million. In Q4 2022, we recognized \$8 million of that amount. The \$8 million corresponded to the options for European and certain Asian territories.

**MR. HARWICK:** On what basis was the \$8 million recognized?

**DR. HALPERN:** We concluded that Aethon had constructively exercised certain of the territorial options based on email communications and course of conduct. Under ASC 606, when we assessed the transaction, we concluded that the option exercise constituted a contract modification that gave rise to additional performance obligations that had been satisfied, and the \$8 million was recognizable.

**MR. HARWICK:** Can you elaborate on what you mean by \"constructive exercise\"?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. There was an email exchange with Aethon --- I believe it was in October 2022 --- in which Aethon discussed their plans for the European and Asian markets. They were talking about timelines for regulatory submissions, commercial launch planning, and market access strategy in those territories. Based on those communications, and Rob Falcone\'s legal analysis of the contract language, we concluded that Aethon had effectively committed to exercising those options. They were acting as though they had exercised the options --- engaging local regulatory consultants, planning commercial operations --- even though they hadn\'t formally submitted a written exercise notice.

**MR. HARWICK:** Was there a formal written exercise notice from Aethon?

**DR. HALPERN:** Not a formal notice per se. It was based on the totality of the communications and the course of dealing between the parties.

**MR. HARWICK:** Whose idea was it to characterize these emails as constructive exercise?

**DR. HALPERN:** It was a collaborative judgment. I discussed it with Rob Falcone and Anya Petrova. Rob provided the legal analysis --- he reviewed the contract language, which did not require a specific form of exercise notice, and he concluded that the course of dealing constituted exercise under the contract. Anya was involved because of the strategic significance of the Aethon relationship. And I handled the accounting treatment. We all agreed it was the right call.

**MR. HARWICK:** You said Mr. Falcone concluded that the course of dealing constituted exercise. Was Mr. Falcone fully supportive of this position?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. Rob was fully on board. He agreed that the email exchange met the contractual standard for exercise. He provided a written analysis that was incorporated into the revenue recognition memo, and he was comfortable with the conclusion.

**MR. HARWICK:** And can you describe the revenue recognition memo for this item?

**DR. HALPERN:** The memo was prepared by Derek Yoon\'s team. It laid out the facts --- the email exchange, Aethon\'s commercial activities in the relevant territories, the contract language regarding option exercise --- and it concluded that the options had been constructively exercised. Rob Falcone\'s legal analysis was attached to the memo as an exhibit. I personally reviewed that memo, as I did with all significant memos, and I signed off on it. I was satisfied that the analysis was sound and the conclusion was supportable.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did Stanton Barrow review this treatment?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. We discussed the constructive exercise treatment with Stanton Barrow during the Q4 2022 review process. They reviewed the analysis, including Rob\'s legal memorandum, and they were comfortable with it.

**MR. HARWICK:** I\'d like to explore the constructive exercise theory in a bit more detail.

**[4.6 Discussion of the Constructive Exercise Theory in Detail]{.underline}**

**MR. HARWICK:** Dr. Halpern, can you walk me through the specific factual basis for the constructive exercise conclusion? What exactly was Aethon doing that led you to conclude they had constructively exercised the options?

**DR. HALPERN:** Several things. First, the email exchange I mentioned --- Aethon\'s senior leadership was communicating with our team about their plans for the European and Asian territories. They were discussing specific timelines. They referenced \"moving forward\" with the territorial expansion. They were not hedging or expressing uncertainty --- the tone and substance of the communications indicated they had made the decision to proceed.

Second, Aethon had taken concrete steps that were consistent with having exercised the options. They had engaged local regulatory consultants in several of the relevant territories. They were planning commercial operations --- hiring local personnel, setting up distribution infrastructure. These were not the actions of a company that was still deliberating about whether to exercise its options. These were the actions of a company that had committed to a course of action.

Third, and this is where Rob\'s analysis was key, the contract language regarding option exercise was not narrowly prescriptive. It did not say, for example, that the options could only be exercised by delivery of a signed written notice in a particular form. The language was more general. Rob\'s interpretation was that the contract contemplated exercise through conduct, not just through formal documentation, and that the totality of Aethon\'s communications and actions constituted exercise.

**MR. HARWICK:** But Aethon never signed a formal exercise notice?

**DR. HALPERN:** No, but the contract didn\'t require a specific form of notice. Rob Falcone reviewed the contract language and concluded that the course of dealing constituted exercise. That was the legal analysis, and I relied on it.

**MR. HARWICK:** You say you relied on Mr. Falcone\'s analysis. Was this primarily a legal judgment in your view?

**DR. HALPERN:** The question of whether the options had been exercised was really Rob\'s call from a legal interpretation standpoint. I relied on his judgment regarding the contract terms. My role was to take that legal conclusion and translate it into the appropriate accounting treatment under ASC 606. But the threshold question --- had the options been exercised --- that was a legal determination, and Rob made it.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did you consult with Stanton Barrow specifically on the constructive exercise theory?

**DR. HALPERN:** Yes. We discussed the treatment with them, and they were comfortable with it. Richard Muñoz and his team reviewed the analysis, including the legal memo, and they did not object. They asked questions --- they wanted to understand the factual basis and the legal reasoning --- but ultimately they were comfortable.

**MR. HARWICK:** Did anyone at Crestline express concerns or disagreement with the constructive exercise theory?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. Not

that I recall. Everyone was aligned. Rob, Anya, myself --- we were all comfortable with the position. And, as I said, Stanton Barrow was comfortable as well. There was no dissent.

**MR. HARWICK:** No one raised any red flags or suggested that the company should wait for formal exercise before recognizing the revenue?

**DR. HALPERN:** No. The collective judgment was that the options had been exercised based on the course of dealing, and we accounted for it accordingly.

**MR. HARWICK:** Thank you, Dr. Halpern. Let me shift to a different topic.

That was how I managed.

I\'ve seen CFOs who take a more removed, strategic approach --- they set the direction and let the team handle the details. That\'s not how I operated. I was in the weeds on the things that mattered, and revenue recognition was at the top of that list. These were among the most consequential accounting judgments we made. **DR. HALPERN:** For every significant revenue recognition judgment, I would review the memo, ask questions if I had them, and make the final call. I didn\'t just rubber-stamp things. **[SECTION 2: OVERVIEW OF REVENUE RECOGNITION PRACTICES AT CRESTLINE]{.underline}**

**BY MS. ASHFORD:**

**Q.** Dr. Halpern, I\'d like to turn now to revenue recognition practices at Crestline generally. Are you familiar with Accounting Standards Codification Topic 606 --- Revenue from Contracts with Customers?

**A.** Yes. ASC 606 is the revenue recognition standard.

**Q.** Can you describe at a high level the framework that Crestline applied under ASC 606?

**A.** Sure. ASC 606 uses a five-step model for revenue recognition. Step one is to identify the contract with the customer. Step two is to identify the performance obligations in the contract --- the distinct goods or services that the entity has promised to deliver. Step three is to determine the transaction price --- essentially, how much consideration the entity expects to receive. Step four is to allocate that transaction price to the individual performance obligations. And step five is to recognize revenue when, or as, the entity satisfies each performance obligation.

**Q.** In the context of Crestline\'s business, what types of contracts typically involved ASC 606 analysis?

**A.** The primary contracts that involved significant ASC 606 analysis were our licensing agreements, our co-development agreements, and our partnership agreements with pharmaceutical companies and biotech firms. These agreements often included multiple elements --- upfront license fees, milestone payments tied to clinical or regulatory achievements, royalties, and cost-sharing provisions. Allocating the transaction price and determining when performance obligations were satisfied required significant judgment.

**Q.** When you say \"significant judgment,\" can you explain what you mean?

**A.** I mean that these weren\'t straightforward transactions. They weren\'t sales of widgets where you ship a product and recognize revenue. These were complex, multi-element arrangements where you had to evaluate whether individual components were distinct performance obligations, whether milestone payments were constrained variable consideration, and when specific performance criteria had been met. Those determinations required careful analysis and professional judgment.

**Q.** Did Crestline have written policies and procedures for revenue recognition?

**A.** Yes. We had formal revenue recognition policies that were part of our accounting policies manual. We also had a practice of preparing revenue recognition memoranda for significant transactions, which documented the analysis under ASC 606 and the basis for the recognition conclusion.

**Q.** Who prepared those revenue recognition memoranda?

**A.** Derek Yoon, our Director of Financial Reporting, was the primary drafter. He would prepare the initial draft of the memorandum, including the technical analysis under ASC 606. Janet Liang, our controller, would review and approve the memo. And then for significant items, I would review and sign off.

**Q.** How did you determine which items were \"significant\" and therefore warranted your review?

**A.** Generally, any revenue recognition involving a new partnership agreement or a milestone payment over a certain threshold --- I believe it was \$1 million --- would come to me for review. There were also qualitative factors. If the judgment was particularly complex or if there was a novel accounting question, that would warrant my review as well.

**Q.** And what was your role in reviewing those memos?

**A.** I would review the significant ones at a high level. My team --- Derek Yoon in particular --- prepared the detailed analysis. I trusted their judgment on the technical details. I was more focused on the business context --- making sure the memo reflected the economic substance of the transaction and that the team had considered the relevant contractual provisions.

**Q.** Did you personally sign off on revenue recognition memos?

**A.** I signed off on the more significant ones, yes. But I want to be clear --- my signature reflected my reliance on the team\'s analysis rather than an independent line-by-line review. I was comfortable that the team had done the work and that the conclusions were reasonable.

**Q.** Did you ever disagree with the team\'s conclusion in a revenue recognition memo?

**A.** There may have been occasions where I asked questions or sought additional information. But I don\'t recall a situation where I fundamentally disagreed with the team\'s conclusion and overrode it. The process was collaborative.

The government focused its questioning on a \$5.2 million milestone payment that was recognized as revenue in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Q4 2021). This milestone was tied to first-patient enrollment in the Phase II clinical trial for compound CRT-4400, which was being conducted under the Meridian partnership.

AUSA Colwell asked Halpern when he first became aware that the enrollment milestone had been achieved. Halpern stated: \"We received confirmation from the Meridian project team before Christmas 2021, I believe in the December 20th timeframe.\" This was noted by counsel as a direct quote.

First, the date has progressively moved later with e

ach successive account --- from late November, to mid-December, to December 20. Second, the level of specificity has paradoxically increased even as the temporal distance from the event has grown. All three stated dates precede the actual confirmed first-patient enrollment date, which the Audit Committee investigation and restatement concluded did not occur until February 2022. The progressive movement of the stated date creates an appearance that Dr. Halpern is incrementally retreating toward the actual timeline while attempting to maintain that the recognition was appropriate as of Q4 2021.

**[V.B. Aethon Compound Delivery Milestone --- \$7.1 Million (Q3 2022)]{.underline}**

The government devoted substantial time to questioning Halpern about the \$7.1 million milestone payment recognized in the third quarter of 2022 (Q3 2022). In the November 2, 2023 Audit Committee interview, Halpern stated that he \"first learned that compound delivery to Aethon was incomplete\" only when the Audit Committee investigation commenced in October 2023 --- a position of complete denial of prior knowledge. In the April 16, 2024 SEC deposition, when confronted with the September 19, 2022 email from Janet Liang (which stated: \"Only 3 of 5 batches delivered. Three materially different accounts have now been provided --- (1) no knowledge, (2) received the email but didn\'t focus on it, (3) general awareness plus affirmative justification --- and the government has all three on record.

The government followed up by specifically referencing the September 19, 2022 email from Janet Liang to Halpern, in which Liang wrote: \"Only 3 of 5 batches delivered. Should we hold Q3 recognition?\" The government asked Halpern to confirm that he received this email and to describe his response.

Halpern acknowledged receiving the email and stated that he recalled it \"in general terms.\" He stated that the email was one of many operational updates he received from Liang on a daily basis during the quarter-end period and that it did not strike him at the time as raising a significant issue because he believed the delivery was substantially complete.

The government then turned to Halpern\'s September 22, 2022 reply email to Liang, in which Halpern wrote: \"Let\'s discuss offline. I think we can make the case that delivery is substantially complete.\"

The government asked: \"Did you have an offline conversation with Ms. Liang about this?\"

Halpern stated: \"Yes, I believe we did speak about it briefly. Janet and I discussed the delivery status, and she agreed the delivery was substantially complete and recognition was appropriate.\"

*Counsel observation --- CRITICAL:* This statement directly contradicts Dr. Halpern\'s testimony in the April 16, 2024 SEC deposition. In that deposition, when asked the same question about whether the offline conversation occurred, Halpern testified that the conversation never took place because \"things got busy and it fell through the cracks.\" He explicitly stated in the deposition that the conversation \"never happened.\" Now, in the proffer, he states not only that the conversation did occur but that Liang affirmatively agreed with the recognition decision. These accounts are irreconcilable. If the conversation occurred (as Halpern now claims), his SEC deposition testimony that it \"never happened\" constitutes a false statement in a sworn proceeding. If the conversation did not occur (as he previously testified), his proffer statement is false and potentially a violation of the truthfulness requirement of the proffer agreement. Moreover, Halpern\'s claim that Liang \"agreed\" with the recognition decision introduces a factual assertion that is subject to independent verification. If Janet Liang testifies that the conversation occurred but that she pushed back on or disagreed with the recognition (or if she corroborates the SEC deposition account that the conversation never happened), Halpern\'s credibility will be severely damaged on a central issue. This inconsistency is among the most dangerous in the entire record.

Halpern further stated that the concept of \"substantially complete delivery\" was, in his view, consistent with ASC 606 principles regarding the satisfaction of performance obligations. He described the accounting standard as permitting recognition when a performance obligation is \"substantially satisfied\" and stated that, in his judgment, delivery of three of five compound batches represented a level of completion that warranted recognition because the remaining batches were not material to the overall arrangement.

The government asked whether the remaining two of five batches were material. Halpern stated that he \"did not consider them material to the overall transaction\" at the time the recognition decision was made. **[V.C. Aethon Territorial Option Fees --- \$8 Million (Q4 2022)]{.underline}**

The government next turned to the \$8 million in territorial option fees recognized in the fourth quarter of 2022 (Q4 2022). Under the Aethon Agreement, Aethon held options to acquire exclusive commercialization rights in specified ex-U.S. territories. The exercise of those options would trigger payment of fees totaling \$15 million, of which Crestline recognized \$8 million in Q4 2022.

**Basis for Recognition**

Halpern described the basis for the Q4 2022 recognition as follows: \"We had a series of email exchanges with Aethon in October 2022 that, in our judgment, constituted a constructive exercise of the territorial options for ex-U.S. markets.\" He described these email exchanges as involving Aethon personnel expressing \"strong interest\" in the ex-U.S. territories and beginning to discuss commercial plans, market entry strategies, and regulatory timelines for the territories in question. He stated that Crestline\'s management team --- including himself, Falcone, and Simmons --- reviewed the email exchanges and concluded that Aethon\'s course of conduct amounted to a constructive exercise of the options under the terms of the contract, even though Aethon had not executed a formal exercise notice.

When the government asked specifically whether Aethon had formally signed any exercise notice, Halpern acknowledged: \"No formal exercise notice was signed, but we believed the course of conduct was sufficient.\" He stated that the contract language did not, in his view, require a formal written notice as the exclusive method of exercise, and that the course-of-dealing between the parties supported the conclusion that the options had been constructively exercised.

**The November 14, 2022 Email and Financial Targets**

It is notable that the government did not specifically ask about the November 14, 2022 email from Halpern to Janet Liang and Derek Yoon, in which Halpern wrote: \"If we can book this in Q4, it gets us to the annual guidance number.\" This email has been a focal point of the SEC\'s civil case and is expected to be central to any criminal prosecution as evidence of motive --- specifically, that the \$8 million territorial option recognition was driven by a desire to meet Crestline\'s \$318 million annual revenue guidance target for fiscal year 2022. Despite not being asked about this email, Halpern affirmatively volunteered the following statement:

\"The territorial option recognition was purely an accounting judgment with no connection to financial targets. We analyzed the email exchanges, discussed them with legal, and concluded that Aethon had constructively exercised.\"

*Counsel observation:* The unprompted nature of this denial is notable and, in counsel\'s view, potentially counterproductive. The government had not referenced the November 14, 2022 email or asked any question relating to the connection between the territorial option recognition and Crestline\'s financial targets. By volunteering a denial of a connection that had not been raised, Halpern may have inadvertently drawn the government\'s attention to the vulnerability and signaled his awareness of the significance of the issue. In the April 16, 2024 SEC deposition, when directly confronted with the November 14, 2022 email (which explicitly references the annual revenue guidance number of \$318 million), Halpern characterized the email as a \"casual observation\" that \"didn\'t drive the accounting judgment.\" The proffer statement --- \"purely an accounting judgment with no connection to financial targets\" --- is a stronger denial than the SEC deposition characterization but is made in a context where the question was not asked, which may suggest consciousness of the vulnerability. Prosecutors will argue that the November 14, 2022 email is powerful motive evidence showing that the recognition was driven by a desire to meet the \$318 million guidance number, and that Halpern\'s escalating denials across multiple testimony sessions reflect awareness that the email is damaging. Halpern\'s characterizations across both sessions may be insufficient to neutralize the plain language of the email.

**Role of General Counsel Rob Falcone**

The government asked about the role of General Counsel Rob Falcone in the territorial option recognition decision. Halpern initially stated that Falcone was \"generally involved\" in the decision and had \"reviewed the situation.\" He described Falcone\'s role as providing legal input on the interpretation of the contract terms governing the exercise of the territorial options.

Then, for the first time in any testimony session, Halpern made a significant and previously undisclosed statement. He said: \"I should mention --- I now recall that Rob sent me a text message around that time, in November 2022, saying something to the effect of \'I\'m not comfortable with the constructive exercise theory --- we should get outside counsel involved.\'\"

The government immediately focused on this disclosure. AUSA Colwell asked: \"Did you raise this text message in your prior Audit Committee interview or SEC deposition?\"

Halpern stated: \"I didn\'t recall it at the time. It only came back to me recently when I was reviewing my text messages in preparation for this session.\"

The government pressed further. Trial Attorney Reiter asked: \"Did you seek outside counsel\'s opinion as Mr. Falcone suggested?\"

Halpern responded: \"I don\'t believe we did. I discussed it further with Rob and believed we had resolved his concerns.\"

The government asked Halpern to describe the nature of the subsequent discussion with Falcone in which the concerns were purportedly resolved. Halpern stated that he and Falcone discussed the matter \"further over the next few days\" and that Falcone ultimately \"came around\" to the view that the constructive exercise theory was supportable. Halpern could not provide specific details about the conversation, including the date, location, or substance of the arguments that purportedly persuaded Falcone, nor could he identify any document or communication memorializing the resolution of Falcone\'s concerns.

*Counsel observation --- CRITICAL:* This disclosure raises multiple grave concerns.

> \(a\) **Late Disclosure / Credibility Damage.** The Falcone text message was never mentioned in the November 2, 2023 Audit Committee interview, in which Halpern described Falcone as \"fully supportive\" of the revenue recognition decisions at issue. Nor was it mentioned in the April 16, 2024 SEC deposition, in which Halpern testified that Falcone \"reviewed and approved\" the Q4 2022 territorial option recognition. The claim that Halpern simply \"didn\'t recall\" a text message from his General Counsel explicitly objecting to a \$8 million revenue recognition decision will strain credulity, particularly given the significance of the underlying transaction and the specificity of the objection (\"I\'m not comfortable\... we should get outside counsel involved\"). The late emergence of this text message --- conveniently recalled only after two prior testimony sessions in which it was not disclosed --- will be characterized by prosecutors as deliberate concealment.
>
> \(b\) **Destruction of Reliance-on-Counsel Defense.** A reliance-on-counsel defense requires, among other things, that the defendant sought and relied upon the advice of an attorney. The Falcone text demonstrates that the only attorney Halpern consulted on the constructive exercise theory --- General Counsel Falcone --- expressly disagreed with the theory and recommended seeking outside counsel. Halpern neither followed that recommendation nor obtained outside counsel\'s opinion. The Falcone text thus directly undermines any reliance-on-counsel defense as to Falcone and, in fact, converts it from a defense into an aggravating factor: Halpern was warned by his own lawyer and proceeded anyway.
>
> \(c\) **Notice of Risk.** Prosecutors will argue that the Falcone text put Halpern on notice that the constructive exercise theory was at minimum problematic, and that his decision to proceed with the recognition despite that warning demonstrates recklessness or willful blindness --- or, at the extreme, knowing fraud.
>
> \(d\) **Unverifiable Claim of Resolution.** Halpern\'s assertion that he \"discussed it further with Rob\" and that Falcone \"came around\" is unverifiable in the absence of documentation. If Falcone is subpoenaed and testifies that he did not \"come around\" --- or that no such follow-up conversation occurred --- Halpern\'s account will collapse entirely.
>
> \(e\) **Government\'s Likely Next Steps.** The government will almost certainly subpoena Falcone and seek to obtain the text messages directly. If the text messages are preserved (on either Halpern\'s or Falcone\'s devices or through carrier records), their content may be more damaging than Halpern\'s paraphrase suggests. Defense counsel must immediately obtain copies of Dr. Halpern\'s text messages with Falcone from the November 2022 timeframe and assess the scope and content of those communications.

Halpern confirmed his compensation: \$485,000 base salary, a target annual bonus of 60% of base salary (approximately \$291,000), and equity awards in the form of stock options and restricted stock units. He confirmed that his annual bonus was determined based in part on company financial performance, including revenue targets. When asked to describe the specific metrics, Halpern stated: \"The bonus formula was based on multiple metrics. Revenue was a factor, but not the only one. There were also metrics for clinical pipeline progress, operational efficiency, and individual performance objectives.\"

The government asked Halpern to confirm Crestline\'s market capitalization during the relevant period. Halpern acknowledged that Crestline\'s peak market capitalization was approximately \$1.2 billion, reached in the second quarter of 2022. He further acknowledged that following the November 17, 2023 restatement, Crestline\'s market capitalization declined to approximately \$310 million. The government noted these figures for the record without further commentary.

*Counsel note:* The government is plainly establishing motive through this line of questioning. Halpern had a direct personal financial interest --- through both his bonus (tied in part to revenue targets) and his equity awards (the value of which was tied to Crestline\'s stock price and market capitalization) --- in the revenue recognition decisions at issue. The approximately \$890 million decline in market capitalization from peak to post-restatement underscores the magnitude of the impact. The government will argue at trial that Halpern was personally motivated to accelerate or inflate revenue recognition to meet financial targets, protect the stock price, and maximize his own compensation.

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENT

IAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT** **PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION --- DO NOT DISCLOSE**

**[XI. Counsel Observations and Strategic Notes]{.underline}**

*The following section contains the contemporaneous strategic observations and mental impressions of Daniel Kovacs, Senior Associate, and is prepared at the express direction of Sarah Greenfield, Partner, in anticipation of litigation. This section is expressly protected attorney work product under the work-product doctrine and reflects the mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, and legal theories of counsel.*

**[A. Overall Assessment]{.underline}**

Dr. Halpern was generally cooperative and composed throughout the four-hour proffer session. He was attentive, responded to questions without excessive hesitation, and did not invoke his right to decline to answer at any point (though counsel conferred with him privately on several occasions before he responded to particularly sensitive questions). His demeanor was professional and measured.

However, the substance of Dr. Halpern\'s proffer statements is deeply concerning. Across multiple topics, he made statements that diverge from his prior testimony in material and, in several instances, irreconcilable ways. The proffer session, rather than clarifying Dr. Halpern\'s account or strengthening his defensive position, has created significant new exposure. The inconsistencies documented below will be available to the government for impeachment under the terms of the proffer agreement and, together with the prior testimony inconsistencies, create a compounding credibility problem that will be extremely difficult to manage at trial.

**[B. Key Concerns Identified During the Session]{.underline}**

The following issues were identified during or immediately after the session and are organized by reference number for cross-referencing with the forthcoming impeachment and testimony vulnerability memorandum.

**--- Awareness of Incomplete Compound Delivery (Three Versions).** Dr. Halpern has now provided three materially different accounts of his awareness of the incomplete compound delivery to Aethon as of Q3 2022. Version 1 (Audit Committee interview): no knowledge until October 2023. Version 2 (SEC deposition): received the Liang email but characterized it as routine and did not focus on it. Version 3 (DOJ proffer): general awareness, plus an affirmative assertion that substantial completion was sufficient for recognition under ASC 606. Each version represents a progressive escalation in admitted awareness, coupled with a new defensive theory. The government has all three versions on record and can use them in combination to devastating effect.

**--- The \"Offline Discussion\" with Janet Liang (Direct Contradiction).** This is perhaps the most dangerous inconsistency in the record. In the SEC deposition, Halpern testified that the offline conversation with Liang referenced in his September 22, 2022 email \"never happened\" because \"things got busy and it fell through the cracks.\" In the proffer, Halpern stated that the conversation did occur and that Liang agreed with the recognition decision. These accounts are directly contradictory and cannot be reconciled. One of the two accounts is necessarily false. If the government calls Janet Liang as a witness, her testimony on this point will determine which version is impeached --- but either way, one of Dr. Halpern\'s sworn or proffered accounts will be demonstrated to be false.

**--- Personal Consultation with Auditor Muñoz (Material Retreat).** Halpern retreated from claiming personal consultation with engagement partner Richard Muñoz (as stated in the SEC deposition) to characterizing the auditor interaction as occurring at the \"team level.\" This retreat significantly undermines the reliance-on-auditor defense, which requires personal engagement by the defendant with the professional advisor. The three-step progression --- from \"consulted extensively\" (Audit Committee) to \"personally discussed with Muñoz\" (SEC deposition) to \"not certain whether I personally raised it\" (proffer) --- will be presented by the government as evidence of a collapsing defense.

**--- Meridian Milestone Timing (Three Different Dates).** The date of the Meridian enrollment milestone confirmation has shifted across all three testimony sessions: late November 2021 (Audit Committee), approximately December 14--15 (SEC deposition), and \"the December 20th timeframe\" (proffer). All three dates precede the actual confirmed enrollment date of February 2022. The progressive movement of the date and the paradoxically increasing specificity create a pattern that prosecutors will characterize as incremental retreat toward reality while maintaining the pretense that the recognition was timely.

**--- The November 14, 2022 \"Guidance Number\" Email (Unprompted Denial).** Halpern volunteered, without being asked, a denial that the \$8 million territorial option recognition was connected to financial targets. This unprompted denial draws attention to the vulnerability and signals consciousness of the email\'s significance. The email\'s plain language --- \"If we can book this in Q4, it gets us to the annual guidance number\" --- is powerful motive evidence, and Halpern\'s characterizations across the SEC deposition (\"casual observation\") and the proffer (\"purely an accounting judgment with no connection to financial targets\") may be insufficient to overcome the text of the email itself.

**--- Falcone Text Message (First-Time Disclosure).** The first-time disclosure of Falcone\'s November 2022 text message expressing discomfort with the constructive exercise theory is severely damaging. This information was concealed --- whether deliberately or through purported failure of recollection --- in two prior testimony sessions in which Halpern affirmatively described Falcone as \"fully supportive\" (Audit Committee) and as having \"reviewed and approved\" the recognition (SEC deposition). The text message destroys the reliance-on-counsel defense as to Falcone, puts Halpern on notice that the constructive exercise theory was problematic, and creates an appearance of deliberate concealment across multiple proceedings. The government will almost certainly subpoena Falcone and obtain the text messages directly.

**--- Delegation vs. Personal Involvement (Three Positions).** Halpern\'s characterization of his level of involvement in revenue recognition decisions has shifted across all three sessions: \"hands-on / personally reviewed everything\" (Audit Committee), \"big picture / relied on team\" (SEC deposition), and \"involved in all significant judgments but relied on staff for factual inputs\" (proffer). The middle-ground proffer position appears calculated to avoid the extremes of the two prior accounts but creates a pattern of position-shifting that undermines credibility on the threshold question of Halpern\'s role.

**--- Resignation Timing and Rationale (Shifted Explanation + Consciousness of Guilt Timeline).** Halpern has now given two different primary reasons for his resignation: \"personal and family reasons\" (SEC deposition) and \"strategic differences with Dr. Petrova\" (proffer). The shift in explanation, combined with his acknowledgment that he learned of the SEC complaint from Falcone in August 2023 --- approximately one month before his September 14, 2023 resignation, and before the October 2023 Audit Committee investigation and November 2023 restatement --- creates a timeline that prosecutors will present as powerful evidence of consciousness of guilt.

**--- Board and Audit Committee Reporting (Retreat from \"Fully Informed\").** Halpern admitted in the proffer that he \"may not have highlighted\" the specific Aethon delivery and territorial option issues to the Audit Committee, characterizing them as \"within management\'s normal accounting judgment.\" This is a significant retreat from his Audit Committee interview claim that he \"kept the Board and Audit Committee fully informed of all significant accounting judgments.\" The retreat undermines both the good-faith defense and any argument that the Board shared responsibility for the recognition decisions.

**[C. The Proffer Agreement Testimony Trap]{.underline}**

Most critically, the inconsistencies between the proffer and the prior testimony sessions create a structural double-bind for any trial testimony by Dr. Halpern. The proffer agreement permits the government to use proffer statements for impeachment if Halpern testifies at trial inconsistently with the proffer. The SEC deposition transcript and Audit Committee interview notes are independently available to the government.

This means that on virtually every topic covered in the proffer, Halpern faces impeachment material regardless of the position he takes at trial:

> •If he testifies at trial that the offline conversation with Liang never happened (consistent with the SEC deposition), the government can use his proffer statement that it did happen and Liang agreed.
>
> •If he testifies at trial that the conversation did happen (consistent with the proffer), the government can use his SEC deposition testimony that it never happened.
>
> •If he testifies at trial that he \"personally discussed\" the Aethon delivery issue with Muñoz (consistent with the SEC deposition), the government can use his proffer statement that he is \"not certain\" whether he personally raised it.
>
> •If he testifies at trial consistent with the proffer\'s uncertainty about Muñoz, the government can use his SEC deposition claim of personal discussion.
>
> •Similar traps exist for the Meridian milestone date, the characterization of Falcone\'s role, the level of Audit Committee disclosure, and the reason for resignation.

This dynamic applies to virtually every contested topic in the case. The proffer session has, in practical terms, armed the government with a comprehensive impeachment arsenal that can be deployed regardless of which version of events Dr. Halpern chooses to present at trial. This is the most significant strategic consequence of the proffer session and must be the central focus of trial preparation going forward.

**[D. Immediate Next Steps]{.underline}**

The following action items should be addressed on a priority basis:

> 1.**Comprehensive Testimony Comparison.** A detailed, side-by-side comparison of all three testimony sessions --- the November 2, 2023 Audit Committee interview, the April 16, 2024 SEC deposition, and the August 7, 2024 DOJ proffer --- must be prepared immediately. This comparison should identify every material inconsistency, assess the impeachment significance of each, and evaluate potential explanations or rehabilitative arguments. This analysis will form the core of the forthcoming impeachment and testimony vulnerability memorandum.
>
> 2.**Falcone Text Messages.** Counsel must immediately obtain copies of Dr. Halpern\'s text messages with Rob Falcone from the November 2022 timeframe. The exact content of the Falcone text is critical --- Halpern\'s paraphrase during the proffer may be more or less damaging than the actual text. If the text messages are not preserved on Halpern\'s device, alternative sources (Falcone\'s device, carrier records) must be explored, though the defense team\'s ability to access Falcone\'s records may be limited.
>
> 3.**Janet Liang Assessment.** Counsel must assess whether Janet Liang can be interviewed by the defense team or, if that is not possible, determine her likely testimony through other means. Liang\'s account of the offline conversation (or non-conversation) is dispositive of one of the most critical inconsistencies in the record. If Liang has counsel, a proffer to the defense may be possible. If Liang is cooperating with the government, defense counsel should evaluate the implications.
>
> 4.**Falcone Text Production to Government.** Counsel must determine whether the Falcone text message has already been produced to the government through Crestline\'s document productions, through Falcone\'s own productions (if he has been separately subpoenaed), or through other means. If the government already has the text, its content is known and the damage assessment can proceed. If the government does not yet have it, Dr. Halpern\'s proffer disclosure may have triggered a derivative lead that will result in a subpoena.
>
> 5.**Trial Testimony Strategy.** Counsel must begin the difficult but essential analysis of whether Dr. Halpern should testify at trial at all, given the impeachment exposure created by the three testimony sessions. If the decision is made that Halpern should testify, counsel must develop a strategy for addressing the inconsistencies proactively and must prepare Halpern for the aggressive cross-examination that the proffer has enabled. If the decision is that Halpern should not testify, counsel must evaluate the implications for the defense case and whether the proffer statements will be indirectly usable.

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT** **PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION --- DO NOT DISCLOSE**

**[XII. Appendices / Attachments Referenced]{.underline}**

The following documents are referenced in this memorandum and are maintained in the Halpern Defense case file:

> 1.**Proffer Agreement** (August 7, 2024) --- Queen for a Day agreement executed by Dr. Marcus Halpern, AUSA Diana Colwell, and defense counsel prior to the proffer session. *Filename: proffer-agreement.docx*
>
> 2.**Contemporaneous Handwritten Notes** of Daniel Kovacs --- Notes taken during the August 7, 2024 proffer session. Retained in the physical case file at Greenfield & Associates LLP, 500 West Monroe Street, Suite 3200, Chicago, IL 60661. These notes constitute attorney work product and are not to be disclosed.
>
> 3.**Audit Committee Interview Transcript** --- Transcript/notes of the November 2, 2023 interview of Dr. Marcus Halpern conducted by Harwick Alderman LLP on behalf of the Crestline Therapeutics, Inc. Audit Committee. *Filename: audit-committee-interview-transcript.docx*
>
> 4.**SEC Deposition Transcript** --- Transcript of the April 16, 2024 deposition of Dr. Marcus Halpern in *SEC v. Crestline Therapeutics, Inc. et al.*, No. 1:24-cv-02187 (N.D. Ill.). *Filename: sec-deposition-transcript.docx*
>
> 5.**Key Documents Compilation** --- Compilation of key documents referenced in or relevant to the proffer session, including the September 19, 2022 Liang email, the September 22, 2022 Halpern reply email, the November 14, 2022 Halpern email, and other supporting materials. *Filename: key-documents-compilation.docx*

This memorandum should be read in conjunction with the forthcoming impeachment and testimony vulnerability analysis, which will provide a comprehensive side-by-side comparison of all three testimony sessions and detailed strategic recommendations for trial preparation.

**END OF MEMORANDUM**

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT --- PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION --- DO NOT DISCLOSE. This memorandum reflects the mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, and legal theories of counsel at Greenfield & Associates LLP and is protected by the attorney work-product doctrine. Any inadvertent disclosure does not constitute a waiver of the privilege. © 2024 Greenfield & Associates LLP. All rights reserved.
