**[SELECTED EXCERPTS FROM CIVIL COMPLAINT]{.underline}**

**[\*Securities and Exchange Commission v. Crestline Therapeutics, Inc., Dr. Anya Petrova, and Dr. Marcus Halpern\*]{.underline}**

**Case No. 1:24-cv-02187 (N.D. Ill.)**

**PREFATORY NOTE:** This document comprises selected excerpts from the full civil complaint filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission on March 8, 2024, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division. Paragraph numbering is preserved from the original complaint but is non-consecutive because sections not directly relevant to the defense of Dr. Marcus Halpern --- including allegations solely against Crestline Therapeutics, Inc. as a corporate entity and allegations solely against Dr. Anya Petrova --- have been omitted. The full complaint contains 87 paragraphs; the excerpts below cover approximately paragraphs 1--12, 18--22, 34--58, 65--72, and 78--87. This excerpt is compiled for use by the defense team of Greenfield & Associates LLP in connection with the representation of Dr. Marcus Halpern.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF ILLINOIS EASTERN DIVISION

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION,**   
  ----------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Plaintiff,                                

  v\.                                       Case No. 1:24-cv-02187

  **CRESTLINE THERAPEUTICS, INC.,**         **COMPLAINT FOR VIOLATIONS OF**

  **DR. ANYA PETROVA, and**                 **THE FEDERAL SECURITIES LAWS**

  **DR. MARCUS HALPERN,**                   

  Defendants.                               Filed: March 8, 2024
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

**[I. SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS]{.underline}**

1\. The Securities and Exchange Commission (\"Commission\" or \"SEC\") brings this civil enforcement action against Crestline Therapeutics, Inc. (\"Crestline\" or \"the Company\"), a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business at 200 Innovation Drive, Suite 1400, Evanston, Illinois 60201; Crestline\'s Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Anya Petrova (\"Petrova\"); and Crestline\'s former Chief Financial Officer, Dr. Marcus Halpern (\"Halpern\") (collectively, \"Defendants\"), for their roles in a scheme to fraudulently overstate Crestline\'s reported revenue by a total of \$20.3 million across fiscal years 2021 and 2022 through the premature and improper recognition of revenue from two partnership agreements. Defendants accomplished this fraud through the knowing or reckless misapplication of Accounting Standards Codification Topic 606, *Revenue from Contracts with Customers* (\"ASC 606\"), and Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (\"GAAP\"), in violation of the federal securities laws.

2\. From approximately June 2021 through December 2022, Defendants engaged in a scheme to prematurely recognize revenue from the Meridian BioSciences Partnership Agreement (the \"Meridian Agreement\") and the Aethon Pharma Co-Development Agreement (the \"Aethon Agreement\"), inflating Crestline\'s reported revenue by \$20.3 million across three improperly recognized line items: (i) \$5.2 million in Meridian milestone revenue recognized in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2021 (\"Q4 2021\"); (ii) \$7.1 million in Aethon milestone revenue recognized in the third quarter of fiscal year 2022 (\"Q3 2022\"); and (iii) \$8.0 million in Aethon territorial option fees recognized in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2022 (\"Q4 2022\"). Each of these revenue recognition events was premature and unsupported under ASC 606 and GAAP at the time of recognition.

3\. In total, the two partnership agreements generated \$47.3 million in revenue recognized by Crestline across FY2021 and FY2022, consisting of: \$12 million in Meridian upfront license fees; \$5.2 million in Meridian milestone payments; \$15 million in Aethon upfront payments; \$7.1 million in Aethon milestone payments; and \$8 million in Aethon territorial option fees. Of this total amount, \$27 million --- comprising the two upfront payments --- was properly recognized and is not challenged by the Commission. The remaining \$20.3 million was improperly and prematurely recognized and was subsequently restated by the Company.

4\. Defendant Halpern, as Chief Financial Officer of Crestline from March 2018 through his resignation on September 14, 2023, was the senior-most financial officer of the Company. Halpern held an active Certified Public Accountant license issued by the State of Illinois (License No. 065-041882), possessed a Master of Business Administration degree from a leading business school, and had extensive experience in financial reporting at public companies, including prior service as Vice President of Finance at Praxon Medical Devices from 2011 to 2018. In his capacity as CFO, Halpern was directly responsible for the Company\'s financial reporting, the development and implementation of revenue recognition policies, the maintenance of internal controls over financial reporting, and the certification of financial statements filed with the Commission.

5\. Halpern\'s annual compensation included a base salary of \$485,000, a target annual bonus equal to 60% of his base salary (approximately \$291,000), and equity awards in the form of restricted stock units and stock options. Halpern\'s bonus was tied in significant part to Crestline\'s achievement of financial targets, including the Company\'s annual revenue guidance. Crestline\'s FY2022 annual revenue guidance target, as publicly disseminated to analysts and investors, was \$318 million. The improper revenue recognition described herein --- totaling \$20.3 million over the two fiscal years, including \$15.1 million recognized in FY2022 alone --- directly contributed to Crestline\'s ability to meet or closely approach that annual revenue guidance target, thereby enhancing Halpern\'s personal financial interests in the form of both bonus compensation and the value of his equity holdings.

6\. Crestline\'s common stock was registered with the Commission pursuant to Section 12(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the \"Exchange Act\") and traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the ticker symbol \"CRST.\" During the period of the fraud, the Company\'s market capitalization peaked at approximately \$1.2 billion in the second quarter of 2022, a period during which its reported revenue was materially overstated as a result of the fraudulent scheme described herein. Following the Company\'s November 17, 2023, restatement announcement, filed with the Commission on Form 8-K, Crestline\'s market capitalization declined precipitously to approximately \$310 million, destroying approximately \$890 million in shareholder value.

*\[Paragraphs 7--8, identifying Crestline Therapeutics, Inc. as a corporate defendant, are omitted from this excerpt.\]*

*\[Paragraph 9, identifying Dr. Anya Petrova, is omitted from this excerpt.\]*

10\. Defendant Dr. Marcus Halpern (\"Halpern\"), age 54, resides at 1842 Lakeview Terrace, Winnetka, Illinois 60093. Halpern served as the Chief Financial Officer of Crestline from March 2018 to September 14, 2023. Halpern holds an active Illinois CPA license (License No. 065-041882) and a Master of Business Administration degree. As CFO, Halpern was Crestline\'s principal financial officer and was responsible for overseeing the Company\'s financial reporting functions, including the preparation and review of financial statements incorporated into the Company\'s periodic reports filed with the Commission. Throughout his tenure as CFO, Halpern signed Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (\"SOX\") Section 302 and Section 906 certifications for Crestline\'s annual reports on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, including the certifications accompanying the FY2021 Form 10-K filed on March 16, 2022, and the FY2022 Form 10-K filed on March 15, 2023. Each of these certifications attested, among other things, that the financial statements contained in the reports fairly presented, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations of the Company.

11\. The Commission brings this action alleging violations of: (a) Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 (the \"Securities Act\") \[15 U.S.C. § 77q(a)\]; (b) Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the \"Exchange Act\") \[15 U.S.C. § 78j(b)\] and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder \[17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5\]; (c) Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act \[15 U.S.C. § 78m(a)\] and Rules 13a-1 and 13a-13 promulgated thereunder \[17 C.F.R. §§ 240.13a-1, 240.13a-13\] (periodic reporting violations); and (d) Exchange Act Rule 13a-14 \[17 C.F.R. § 240.13a-14\] (SOX certifications). The claims against each defendant and the statutory bases therefor are set forth in greater detail below.

12\. Against Defendant Halpern individually, the Commission alleges violations of Securities Act Section 17(a), Exchange Act Section 10(b), and Rule 10b-5, as well as liability for aiding and abetting the Company\'s violations of Exchange Act Section 13(a) and Rules 13a-1 and 13a-13, and for violations of Exchange Act Rule 13a-14 relating to false SOX certifications. The Commission seeks permanent injunctive relief restraining Halpern from future violations of the federal securities laws, disgorgement of all ill-gotten gains including bonuses and equity-based compensation received during the period of the fraud together with prejudgment interest thereon, civil monetary penalties, and an order barring Halpern from serving as an officer or director of any public company.

*\[Paragraphs 13--17 are omitted from this excerpt.\]*

**[II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE]{.underline}**

18\. The Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Sections 20(b) and 22(a) of the Securities Act \[15 U.S.C. §§ 77t(b), 77v(a)\] and Sections 21(d) and 27 of the Exchange Act \[15 U.S.C. §§ 78u(d), 78aa\]. The Commission seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement, civil monetary penalties, and other equitable relief as authorized under these provisions.

19\. This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendant Halpern because he resides in this District, specifically in Winnetka, Illinois, and because the fraudulent conduct alleged herein occurred substantially within this District, including at Crestline\'s corporate headquarters located at 200 Innovation Drive, Suite 1400, Evanston, Illinois, where Halpern maintained his principal office throughout his tenure as CFO.

20\. Venue is proper in this District pursuant to Section 22(a) of the Securities Act \[15 U.S.C. § 77v(a)\] and Section 27 of the Exchange Act \[15 U.S.C. § 78aa\] because certain of the acts, practices, transactions, and courses of business constituting the violations alleged herein occurred within this District, and because Defendants Crestline and Halpern reside in and transact business in this District. Crestline is headquartered in Evanston, Illinois, and Halpern resides in Winnetka, Illinois, both of which are within the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division.

21\. In connection with the acts, practices, and courses of business alleged herein, Defendants, directly or indirectly, made use of the means or instrumentalities of interstate commerce, including but not limited to interstate telephone calls, electronic mail, the internet, and interstate deliveries, or of the mails, or of the facilities of a national securities exchange, in furtherance of the fraudulent scheme described herein.

22\. Crestline\'s securities were listed and traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market, a national securities exchange. Financial statements, annual reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, and current reports on Form 8-K were filed electronically with the Commission through the EDGAR system and were thereby disseminated to investors, analysts, and the public nationwide. Press releases and investor presentations containing the Company\'s financial results were distributed through nationally recognized wire services and made available on the Company\'s investor relations website.

*\[Paragraphs 23--33 are omitted from this excerpt.\]*

**[III. STATEMENT OF FACTS --- THE FRAUDULENT REVENUE RECOGNITION SCHEME]{.underline}**

**A. The Partnership Agreements**

34\. On June 15, 2021, Crestline entered into a Collaboration and Licensing Agreement with Meridian BioSciences, a privately held biotechnology company (the \"Meridian Agreement\"). The total deal value of the Meridian Agreement was \$38 million, structured as follows: (i) a \$12 million upfront license fee payable upon execution; (ii) \$8 million in milestone payments tied to Phase II clinical trial enrollment targets for Crestline\'s proprietary compound CRT-4400; and (iii) \$18 million in co-development cost-sharing obligations payable over the term of the collaboration. Patricia Simmons, Crestline\'s Head of Business Development, led the negotiations for the Meridian Agreement on behalf of the Company.

35\. Crestline recognized the \$12 million Meridian upfront license fee as revenue in the second quarter of fiscal year 2021 (\"Q2 2021\"). The Audit Committee\'s subsequent investigation, conducted by independent counsel from Harwick Alderman LLP, determined that this recognition was appropriate under ASC 606 because the license constituted a distinct performance obligation that was transferred to Meridian upon execution. The Commission does not challenge this recognition.

36\. On January 22, 2022, Crestline entered into a Co-Development Agreement with Aethon Pharma, a multinational pharmaceutical company (the \"Aethon Agreement\"). The total deal value of the Aethon Agreement was \$52 million, structured as follows: (i) a \$15 million upfront payment; (ii) \$22 million in contingent milestone payments tied to Crestline\'s compound delivery obligations; and (iii) \$15 million in option fees for exclusive licenses to specified ex-U.S. territories. Patricia Simmons also led the negotiations for the Aethon Agreement on behalf of Crestline.

37\. Crestline recognized the \$15 million Aethon upfront payment as revenue in the first quarter of fiscal year 2022 (\"Q1 2022\"). The Audit Committee investigation determined that this recognition was appropriate under ASC 606, and the Commission does not challenge this recognition.

38\. The Commission challenges the recognition of three specific revenue items totaling \$20.3 million, each of which was prematurely and improperly recognized in violation of ASC 606 and GAAP: (i) \$5.2 million in Meridian milestone revenue recognized in Q4 2021; (ii) \$7.1 million in Aethon milestone revenue recognized in Q3 2022; and (iii) \$8.0 million in Aethon territorial option fees recognized in Q4 2022. The facts underlying each improper recognition are set forth below.

**B. The Improper Meridian Milestone Recognition --- \$5.2 Million**

39\. Under Section 4.2(b) of the Meridian Agreement, the first milestone payment of \$5.2 million was triggered upon \"confirmed first-patient enrollment\" in a Phase II clinical trial for compound CRT-4400. Under ASC 606, revenue from variable consideration such as milestone payments may be recognized only when (i) the milestone event has occurred, and (ii) it is probable that a significant reversal of the cumulative amount of revenue recognized will not occur in future reporting periods. The milestone event triggering the \$5.2 million payment --- confirmed first-patient enrollment --- did not actually occur until February 7, 2022, which was well after the Q4 2021 quarter-end date of December 31, 2021. The enrollment was not confirmed by the clinical trial\'s independent data monitoring committee until that date.

40\. On December 28, 2021, three days before the close of Q4 2021, Halpern reviewed and signed off on a revenue recognition memorandum prepared by Derek Yoon, Director of Financial Reporting, that concluded the \$5.2 million Meridian milestone should be recognized in Q4 2021. The memorandum relied upon a preliminary, unconfirmed enrollment report generated by the clinical trial site --- a report that had not been verified or validated by the clinical trial\'s data monitoring committee as required under the clinical trial protocol. Halpern, as CFO and the Company\'s principal financial officer, was the senior officer responsible for reviewing and approving such revenue recognition memoranda, and he approved the recognition by affixing his signature to the memorandum on December 28, 2021.

41\. Information available to Halpern at the time of his approval indicated that enrollment had not been confirmed. The revenue recognition memorandum itself noted, on its second page, that the enrollment report was \"preliminary\" and \"subject to verification by the data monitoring committee.\" A reasonable CFO exercising professional judgment under ASC 606 would not have recognized this revenue based on an unconfirmed, preliminary report, particularly given the materiality of the \$5.2 million amount, which represented approximately 1.6% of Crestline\'s FY2021 total revenue. The constraints on variable consideration under ASC 606-10-32-11 required that recognition be deferred until it was probable that a significant reversal would not occur --- a standard that could not be met on the basis of a preliminary and unverified enrollment report.

42\. The Audit Committee investigation conducted by Harwick Alderman LLP concluded that the \$5.2 million Meridian milestone should not have been recognized in Q4 2021 because the milestone event --- confirmed first-patient enrollment --- had not occurred as of the quarter-end date. The milestone revenue was subsequently recognized in Q1 2022, following confirmed enrollment on February 7, 2022, and verification by the data monitoring committee.

**C. The Improper Aethon Milestone Recognition --- \$7.1 Million**

43\. Under Section 5.1(a) of the Aethon Agreement, the \$7.1 million milestone payment was triggered upon Crestline\'s delivery of five specified batches of a proprietary compound (CRT-7750) to Aethon\'s designated manufacturing facility. Delivery of all five batches constituted a single, indivisible performance obligation under the Aethon Agreement and under ASC 606. Revenue may be recognized under ASC 606 only when the performance obligation --- here, delivery of all five compound batches --- is satisfied. As of the Q3 2022 quarter-end date (September 30, 2022), only three of the five required batches had been delivered to Aethon. The remaining two batches were not delivered until October 14 and October 22, 2022, respectively.

44\. On September 19, 2022, eleven days before the Q3 2022 quarter-end, Janet Liang, Crestline\'s Vice President of Revenue Operations and Corporate Controller, sent an email to Halpern in which she expressly stated: \"Only 3 of 5 batches delivered. Should we hold Q3 recognition?\" This email put Halpern on direct and explicit notice that the performance obligation underlying the \$7.1 million milestone was incomplete and that recognition of the milestone revenue in Q3 2022 was premature. Liang, as the Company\'s Corporate Controller, was the second-most senior accounting officer after Halpern and was directly responsible for the day-to-day revenue accounting operations.

45\. On September 22, 2022, three days after receiving Liang\'s email, Halpern responded by email: \"Let\'s discuss offline. I think we can make the case that delivery is substantially complete.\" Rather than directing his finance team to defer recognition of the \$7.1 million milestone pending completion of the delivery obligation, Halpern moved the discussion off of the email record and advocated for recognition of the full milestone revenue despite his knowledge that 40% of the required deliverables --- two of the five compound batches --- had not yet been provided to Aethon.

46\. Halpern\'s assertion that delivery was \"substantially complete\" was inconsistent with the express terms of the Aethon Agreement, which required delivery of all five compound batches as a condition to the milestone payment, and was inconsistent with ASC 606, which requires satisfaction of the performance obligation as defined in the contract between the parties. The Aethon Agreement contained no provision permitting \"substantial completion\" in lieu of full delivery of all five specified batches. ASC 606-10-25-30 provides that a performance obligation is satisfied when (or as) the customer obtains control of the promised asset, and Section 5.1(a) of the Aethon Agreement unambiguously defined the performance obligation as delivery of five specified batches. Halpern, as a licensed CPA with extensive revenue recognition experience, knew or was reckless in not knowing that the \"substantially complete\" theory was unsupported by the contract or by applicable accounting standards.

47\. Despite the Liang email and the clear incompleteness of the delivery obligation, Halpern caused Crestline to recognize \$7.1 million in Aethon milestone revenue in Q3 2022 (for the quarter ending September 30, 2022). He did so by directing or permitting the finance team to record the revenue based on his \"substantially complete\" theory, overriding the concerns raised by the Company\'s own Corporate Controller. This revenue was reflected in Crestline\'s quarterly report on Form 10-Q for Q3 2022, filed with the Commission on November 9, 2022.

48\. On information and belief, Halpern did not fully and accurately disclose to Crestline\'s outside auditors at Stanton Barrow & Co. LLP (engagement partner Richard Muñoz, CPA) the fact that only three of five compound batches had been delivered as of the September 30, 2022, quarter-end date, or that Crestline\'s own V

P of Revenue Operations and Corporate Controller had questioned whether the \$7.1 million milestone recognition should be deferred to a subsequent quarter. Halpern\'s failure to make full and accurate disclosure to Stanton Barrow deprived the outside auditors of information material to their review and audit judgments regarding the appropriateness of the Q3 2022 revenue recognition.

49\. The Audit Committee investigation conducted by Harwick Alderman LLP concluded that the \$7.1 million Aethon milestone should not have been recognized in Q3 2022 because the compound delivery obligation was incomplete as of the quarter-end date. Only three of the five required batches had been delivered. The revenue was subsequently recognized in Q4 2022 upon delivery of all five batches in October 2022.

**D. The Improper Aethon Territorial Option Recognition --- \$8.0 Million**

50\. Section 8 of the Aethon Agreement granted Aethon options to obtain exclusive licenses for certain ex-U.S. territories (specifically, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan, and certain Asia-Pacific territories) in exchange for territorial option fees totaling \$15 million. The options were exercisable at Aethon\'s sole discretion by delivery of a formal written notice to Crestline in accordance with Section 8.3 of the Aethon Agreement, which specified that \"exercise shall be effected only by written notice delivered in accordance with Section 14.1\" (the Agreement\'s general notice provision). Under ASC 606, option fees could be recognized as revenue only upon the counterparty\'s exercise of the option, as exercise was the event that transferred control of the underlying rights. Aethon had not exercised the territorial options.

51\. In Q4 2022, Crestline management --- at Halpern\'s direction --- recognized \$8.0 million of the territorial option fees on the theory that certain informal email exchanges between Crestline\'s business development team (led by Patricia Simmons) and Aethon representatives constituted \"constructive exercise\" of the territorial options. However, no formal written exercise notice was ever delivered by Aethon in accordance with Section 8.3 of the Aethon Agreement. The email exchanges referenced by Crestline in support of recognition were preliminary discussions about Aethon\'s potential interest in exercising the options for European Union and United Kingdom territories, not exercises of the options themselves. The emails contained language such as \"we are evaluating\" and \"likely to move forward,\" which fell far short of constituting an exercise of contractual rights.

52\. On November 14, 2022, Halpern sent an email to Robert Falcone (Crestline\'s General Counsel) and Dr. Anya Petrova (CEO) in which he stated: \"The email exchange with Aethon from October looks like constructive exercise to me. If we can book this in Q4, it gets us to the annual guidance number.\" This email reveals that Halpern\'s motivation for recognizing the \$8 million territorial option fee was not based on a good-faith application of ASC 606 or a genuine assessment of whether the territorial options had been exercised by Aethon, but rather on a desire to meet Crestline\'s FY2022 annual revenue guidance target of \$318 million. The email demonstrates that Halpern viewed the \$8 million recognition as the instrument by which Crestline would reach its publicly stated revenue target, and that his advocacy for the \"constructive exercise\" theory was driven by the Company\'s financial objectives rather than by any principled accounting analysis.

53\. On information and belief, prior to the Q4 2022 recognition of the \$8 million in territorial option fees, Crestline\'s General Counsel Robert Falcone expressed reservations about the constructive exercise theory and suggested that outside counsel be consulted to assess whether the email exchanges between the parties constituted a legally effective exercise of the territorial options under the Aethon Agreement. Halpern proceeded with the recognition notwithstanding Falcone\'s reservations, and outside counsel was not consulted prior to the recognition of revenue.

54\. The Aethon Agreement contained an express provision requiring written notice for exercise of territorial options. Specifically, Section 8.3 of the Aethon Agreement provided that Aethon \"may exercise any Option hereunder by delivering written notice to Crestline in accordance with Section 14.1 hereof, specifying the Territory or Territories for which the Option is being exercised.\" No such written notice was ever delivered by Aethon to Crestline at any time prior to the Q4 2022 recognition (or thereafter). Crestline\'s unilateral characterization of informal, exploratory email exchanges as \"constructive exercise\" was without contractual basis and was inconsistent with ASC 606\'s requirement that revenue be recognized based on the transfer of control in accordance with the terms of the contract between the parties.

55\. Halpern\'s training and experience as a Certified Public Accountant (Illinois License No. 065-041882), his more than two decades of experience in financial reporting at public companies --- including seven years as VP of Finance at Praxon Medical Devices and over five years as CFO of Crestline --- and his direct role in establishing Crestline\'s revenue recognition policies render it implausible that he genuinely believed the informal email exchanges between the business development teams constituted an exercise of the territorial options or that recognition of \$8 million in territorial option fees on that basis was consistent with ASC 606. His professional qualifications negate any claim that the \"constructive exercise\" theory was adopted in good faith.

56\. Crestline had publicly issued FY2022 annual revenue guidance of \$318 million in its Q4 2021 earnings call and reiterated that guidance in subsequent quarterly earnings calls throughout FY2022. Without the \$8 million territorial option recognition in Q4 2022, Crestline would have fallen materially short of that guidance target, creating significant risk of an adverse market reaction and potential analyst downgrades. Halpern was aware of this shortfall and its potential consequences, and, as evidenced by his November 14, 2022, email to Falcone and Petrova, the recognition of the \$8 million was motivated by a desire to \"get\[\] us to the annual guidance number\" rather than by any legitimate application of accounting judgment under ASC 606.

57\. Halpern\'s target annual bonus of \$291,000 --- representing 60% of his \$485,000 base salary --- was tied in part to Crestline\'s financial performance against revenue targets as set forth in the Company\'s executive compensation plan. The recognition of the \$8 million territorial option fee thus directly served Halpern\'s personal financial interest by increasing the likelihood that Crestline would meet the revenue targets upon which his annual bonus was calculated. In addition, Halpern held equity awards (restricted stock units and stock options) whose value was directly tied to the price of Crestline\'s common stock, which in turn was influenced by the Company\'s reported financial performance.

58\. The Audit Committee investigation conducted by Harwick Alderman LLP concluded that the \$8 million Aethon territorial option fee should not have been recognized in Q4 2022 because Aethon had not exercised the territorial options as required by Section 8.3 of the Aethon Agreement. No formal written notice of exercise had been delivered by Aethon to Crestline. As of the date of the restatement announcement on November 17, 2023, Aethon still had not exercised the territorial options, and no formal written notice of exercise had been received by Crestline at any time.

*\[Paragraphs 59--64 are omitted from this excerpt.\]*

**[IV. HALPERN\'S SCIENTER]{.underline}**

65\. Defendant Halpern acted with scienter --- that is, with an intent to deceive, manipulate, or defraud, or with severe recklessness --- in causing Crestline to prematurely and improperly recognize \$20.3 million in revenue as described above. The following facts, individually and collectively, establish that Halpern possessed the requisite mental state at the time of each improper recognition and at the time he signed the SOX certifications described below.

66\. *Actual Knowledge of Incomplete Delivery (Aethon \$7.1M).* Halpern received the September 19, 2022, email from Liang, Crestline\'s VP of Revenue Operations and Corporate Controller, expressly stating that only three of five compound batches had been delivered and questioning whether recognition of the \$7.1 million milestone should be deferred to a subsequent period. Despite this actual and direct notice, Halpern directed recognition to proceed in Q3 2022. His September 22, 2022, reply email --- \"Let\'s discuss offline. I think we can make the case that delivery is substantially complete\" --- demonstrates that Halpern was aware of the facts that made recognition improper, understood that the recognition was questionable, and consciously chose to proceed on the basis of an accounting rationale that was unsupported by the contract or by ASC 606.

67\. *The Guidance Number as Motive.* Halpern\'s November 14, 2022, email to Falcone and Petrova --- \"If we can book this in Q4, it gets us to the annual guidance number\" --- is direct evidence that the \$8 million territorial option recognition was driven by Crestline\'s need to meet its publicly stated \$318 million FY2022 annual revenue guidance target, and not by any good-faith accounting judgment regarding whether the territorial options had been exercised. This email links the improper recognition to the Company\'s financial targets and demonstrates that Halpern viewed revenue recognition as a tool for achieving business objectives rather than as a faithful application of GAAP and ASC 606. The email was written by the Company\'s most senior financial officer, at a time when he was in full possession of the relevant facts --- including the absence of any formal exercise notice from Aethon.

68\. *Professional Expertise Negating Good Faith.* Halpern was a licensed CPA with over two decades of financial reporting experience at publicly traded companies. His expertise in ASC 606 and revenue recognition standards is evidenced by the fact that he played a leading role in establishing Crestline\'s revenue recognition policies upon joining the Company as CFO in March 2018, including the Company\'s transition to ASC 606 from the prior revenue recognition standard. A professional of Halpern\'s training and experience either knew, or was severely reckless in not knowing, that: (a) recognizing \$5.2 million in milestone revenue based on an unconfirmed, preliminary enrollment report was improper under ASC 606\'s constraints on variable consideration; (b) recognizing \$7.1 million in milestone revenue when 40% of the contractually required deliverables were outstanding was improper because the performance obligation was not satisfied; and (c) characterizing informal, exploratory emails as \"constructive exercise\" of contractual options requiring written notice was improper and inconsistent with both the contract terms and ASC 606.

69\. *Financial Motive.* Halpern\'s compensation package --- consisting of a \$485,000 base salary, a \$291,000 target annual bonus, and equity awards in the form of restricted stock units and stock options --- created a direct personal financial incentive for Crestline to meet its revenue targets. The \$20.3 million in improperly recognized revenue contributed materially to Crestline\'s reported financial performance, which in turn affected the calculation of Halpern\'s annual bonus and the market value of his equity holdings. Crestline\'s stock price and market capitalization peaked at approximately \$1.2 billion in Q2 2022, during the period when the Company\'s reported revenue was inflated by the improper recognition of the Meridian and Aethon revenue items.

70\. *Internal Warnings Disregarded.* Multiple internal sources flagged concerns to Halpern regarding the propriety of the challenged revenue recognition events, and Halpern disregarded each of them. Janet Liang, Crestline\'s VP of Revenue Operations and Corporate Controller, directly questioned the Q3 2022 Aethon milestone recognition in her September 19, 2022, email. Robert Falcone, Crestline\'s General Counsel, expressed reservations about the constructive exercise theory for the Q4 2022 Aethon territorial option recognition and recommended that outside counsel be consulted. Halpern disregarded both of these internal warnings and proceeded with the improper recognitions without obtaining outside guidance.

71\. *Suspicious Resignation Timing.* Halpern resigned from Crestline on September 14, 2023, approximately one month after being informed by Falcone in August 2023 that the Commission had received a complaint relating to Crestline\'s accounting practices and revenue recognition. Halpern\'s resignation preceded the Audit Committee\'s retention of independent counsel from Harwick Alderman LLP (October 5, 2023) and the Company\'s public restatement announcement (November 17, 2023) by several weeks. The timing of Halpern\'s departure --- after learning of the SEC complaint but before the accounting irregularities were publicly exposed --- is consistent with consciousness of guilt and awareness that the revenue recognition practices he oversaw would not withstand scrutiny.

72\. Taken together, Halpern\'s actual knowledge of the facts making recognition improper, his financial motive to inflate Crestline\'s reported revenue, his disregard of internal warnings from the Corporate Controller and the General Counsel, his extensive professional expertise as a CPA and senior financial officer, the contemporaneous documentary evidence --- including the Liang email, his \"substantially complete\" reply, and the November 14, 2022, \"guidance number\" email --- and the suspicious timing of his resignation establish scienter by a strong preponderance of the evidence and give rise to a strong inference of scienter as required under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (\"PSLRA\").

*\[Paragraphs 73--77 are omitted from this excerpt.\]*

**[V. SOX CERTIFICATION CLAIMS AGAINST HALPERN]{.underline}**

78\. Exchange Act Rule 13a-14 \[17 C.F.R. § 240.13a-14\], implementing Section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, requires the principal financial officer of an issuer that files periodic reports with the Commission to certify in each annual report on Form 10-K and each quarterly report on Form 10-Q that, among other things: (a) the signing officer has reviewed the report; (b) based on the signing officer\'s knowledge, the report does not contain any untrue statement of a material fact or omit to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, in light of the circumstances under which such statements were made, not misleading with respect to the period covered by the report; and (c) based on the signing officer\'s knowledge, the financial statements, and other financial information included in the report, fairly present in all material respects the financial condition and results of operations of the issuer as of, and for, the periods presented in the report.

79\. Section 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, codified at 18 U.S.C. § 1350, separately requires the principal financial officer of an issuer to certify that each periodic report containing financial statements filed with the Commission fully complies with the requirements of Section 13(a) or Section 15(d) of the Exchange Act and that the information contained in the periodic report fairly presents, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations of the issuer. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1350(c)(1), any person who certifies any statement set forth in a Section 906 certification knowing that the periodic report accompanying the statement does not comport with all the requirements set forth in the certification shall be subject to a fine of not more than \$1,000,000, or imprisonment of not more than 10 years, or both. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1350(c)(2), any person who willfully certifies any statement set forth in a Section 906 certification knowing that the periodic report accompanying the statement does not comport with all the requirements set forth in the certification shall be subject to a fine of not more than \$5,000,000, or imprisonment of not more than 20 years, or both.

80\. Halpern signed SOX 302 and 906 certifications in connection with Crestline\'s FY2021 annual report on Form 10-K, filed with the Commission on March 16, 2022. The FY2021 10-K contained financial statements recognizing, *inter alia*, the \$5.2 million Meridian milestone revenue that was subsequently restated by the Company. At the time of Halpern\'s certification, Halpern had reviewed and signed off on the Q4 2021 revenue recognition memorandum (dated December 28, 2021) that relied upon a preliminary, unconfirmed enrollment report, and he knew or was reckless in not knowing that the recognition was premature.

81\. On March 15, 2023, Halpern signed SOX 302 and 906 certifications in connection with Crestline\'s FY2022 annual report on Form 10-K. The FY2022 10-K contained financial statements recognizing, *inter alia*, the \$7.1 million Aethon milestone revenue (recognized in Q3 2022) and the \$8.0 million Aethon territorial option fees (recognized in Q4 2022), both of which were subsequently restated. At the time Halpern signed these certifications, he was in possession of the following information demonstrating that the financial statements incorporated into the FY2022 10-K were materially misstated:

> \(a\) The September 19, 2022, email from Janet Liang, Crestline\'s VP of Revenue Operations and Corporate Controller, informing Halpern that only three of five compound batches had been delivered and questioning whether the \$7.1 million milestone recognition should be deferred;
>
> \(b\) His own September 22, 2022, reply email to Liang, advocating for recognition on a \"substantially complete\" theory despite incomplete delivery;
>
> \(c\) His own November 14, 2022, email to Falcone and Petrova, acknowledging that the \$8 million territorial option recognition would \"get\[\] us to the annual guidance number,\" thereby revealing that recognition was motivated by financial targets rather than accounting substance;
>
> \(d\) The absence of any formal written option exercise notice from Aethon as required by Section 8.3 of the Aethon Agreement, a fact of which Halpern was aware or, at minimum, should have ascertained as the Company\'s principal financial officer before certifying the accuracy of the financial statements; and
>
> \(e\) On information and belief, a text message from Robert Falcone in approximately November 2022 expressing discomfort with the constructive exercise theory and recommending that outside counsel be consulted before recognition.

82\. Halpern\'s SOX 302 and 906 certifications for FY2021 and FY2022 were materially false. The financial statements certified by Halpern contained untrue statements of material fact --- specifically, the premature recognition of \$20.3 million in revenue from the Meridian and Aethon partnership agreements --- and the financial statements did not fairly present, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations of Crestline for the periods covered by the certifications. Halpern knew, or was reckless in not knowing, that the certifications were false based on the information enumerated in the preceding paragraph and the totality of the circumstances described throughout this Complaint.

83\. Halpern cannot claim good faith reliance on Crestline\'s outside auditors, Stanton Barrow & Co. LLP, as a defense to the false certification claims. A reliance defense requires that the defendant made full and accurate disclosure of all material facts to the professional upon whom the defendant claims to have relied. On information and belief, Halpern did not fully and accurately disclose to Stanton Barrow the facts relating to the incomplete Aethon compound delivery, the Liang email questioning the Q3 2022 recognition, or the lack of contractual support for the constructive exercise theory underlying the Q4 2022 recognition. Halpern\'s failure to provide complete and candid information to Crestline\'s auditors precludes any defense premised on reliance on the auditors\' judgment.

84\. By reason of the foregoing conduct, Halpern has demonstrated that he is unfit to serve as an officer or director of a publicly traded company. The Commission seeks an order pursuant to Securities Act Section 20(e) \[15 U.S.C. § 77t(e)\] and Exchange Act Section 21(d)(2) \[15 U.S.C. § 78u(d)(2)\] barring Halpern from acting as an officer or director of any issuer that has a class of securities registered pursuant to Section 12 of the Exchange Act or that is required to file reports pursuant to Section 15(d) of the Exchange Act.

**[VI. CLAIMS FOR RELIEF AGAINST HALPERN]{.underline}**

**Violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933**

**(Against Defendant Halpern)**

essary in order to make the statements made, in light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading, in violation of Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act \[15 U.S.C. § 77q(a)(2)\]; and (c) engaged in transactions, practices, or courses of business which operated or would operate as a fraud or deceit upon the purchasers of such securities, in violation of Section 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act \[15 U.S.C. § 77q(a)(3)\]. **Violations of Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5 Thereunder**

**(Against Defendant Halpern)**

87\. The Commission restates and incorporates by reference each and every allegation contained in paragraphs 1 through 84 above as if fully set forth herein.

88\. Defendant Halpern, directly or indirectly, in connection with the purchase or sale of securities, by the use of means or instrumentalities of interstate commerce, or of the mails, or of any facility of a national securities exchange, with scienter: (a) employed devices, schemes, or artifices to defraud, in violation of Exchange Act Section 10(b) \[15 U.S.C. § 78j(b)\] and Rule 10b-5(a) \[17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5(a)\]; (b) made untrue statements of material fact or omitted to state material facts necessary in order to make the statements made, in light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading, in violation of Exchange Act Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5(b) \[17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5(b)\]; and (c) engaged in acts, practices, or courses of business which operated or would operate as a fraud or deceit upon other persons, in violation of Exchange Act Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5(c) \[17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5(c)\]. **COUNT VII.**

**Aiding and Abetting Crestline\'s Violations of Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act and Rules 13a-1 and 13a-13 Thereunder**

**(Against Defendant Halpern)**

89\. The Commission restates and incorporates by reference each and every allegation contained in paragraphs 1 through 84 above as if fully set forth herein.

90\. Crestline violated Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act \[15 U.S.C. § 78m(a)\] and Rules 13a-1 and 13a-13 promulgated thereunder \[17 C.F.R. §§ 240.13a-1, 240.13a-13\] by filing with the Commission materially false and misleading annual reports on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q for FY2021 and FY2022 that materially overstated the Company\'s revenue by \$20.3 million. **COUNT VIII.**

**(Against Defendant Halpern)**

91\. The Commission restates and incorporates by reference each and every allegation contained in paragraphs 1 through 84 above as if fully set forth herein.
